entries.definition: Occurrence of events by chance in a happy or beneficial way.
examples: Finding that antique bookstore was pure serendipity.
entries.notes: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754.

entries.definition: Lasting for a very short time; transitory.
examples: Fame in the digital era can be strikingly ephemeral.
entries.notes: From Greek ephemeros, meaning lasting only a day.

entries.definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear.
examples: Her mellifluous voice captivated the entire auditorium.
entries.notes: From Latin mel (honey) and fluere (to flow).

entries.definition: The pleasant, earthy scent that accompanies the first rain after a dry spell.
examples: The sweet petrichor filled the evening breeze after months of summer drought.
entries.notes: Coined in 1964 by Australian researchers.

entries.definition: Too great, powerful, or beautiful to be expressed in words.
examples: Standing atop the Himalayan summit gave him a sense of ineffable wonder.
entries.notes: Frequently used in mystical and philosophical texts.

entries.definition: A person who acts obsequiously toward someone important in order to gain advantage.
examples: Surrounded by sycophants, the emperor never heard an honest critique.
entries.notes: Often tested on GRE, SAT, and vocabulary exams.

entries.definition: Mental calmness, composure, and evenness of temper, especially in a difficult situation.
examples: She accepted both praise and harsh criticism with admirable equanimity.
entries.notes: Core virtue in Stoic and Buddhist philosophy.

entries.definition: Present, appearing, or found everywhere simultaneously.
examples: Smartphones have become ubiquitous across the globe.
entries.notes: Derived from Latin ubique, meaning everywhere.

entries.definition: Emission of light by a substance not resulting from heat.
examples: Deep-sea jellyfish display mesmerizing bioluminescence in the abyss.
entries.notes: Includes fluorescence and phosphorescence.

entries.definition: The capacity to withstand or recover quickly from difficult conditions.
examples: The team demonstrated remarkable resilience throughout the challenging season.
entries.notes: From Latin resilire, to spring back.

entries.definition: Again and again in the same way; forever or without end.
examples: They debated the proposed policy ad infinitum without reaching consensus.
entries.notes: Latin phrase widely used in legal and academic arguments.

entries.definition: Undertaken in good faith; genuine, real, without fraud.
examples: She made a bona fide effort to resolve the dispute before filing suit.
entries.notes: Latin for "with good faith".

entries.definition: Seize the day; make the most of the present moment with little concern for the future.
examples: Remember carpe diem when hesitating to pursue your passions.
entries.notes: Originated in Roman poet Horace’s Odes (23 BC).

entries.definition: The existing state of affairs, especially regarding social, cultural, or political issues.
examples: The innovative startup actively sought to disrupt the industry status quo.
entries.notes: Short for status quo ante (the state before the war).

entries.definition: An absence of preconceived ideas or predetermined goals; a clean slate.
examples: The new design lead treated the legacy product architecture as a tabula rasa.
entries.notes: Popularized by John Locke in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding.

entries.definition: Existing in fact or practice, whether recognized by formal law or not.
examples: Although not officially the director, he became the de facto leader of the initiative.
entries.notes: Contrast with de jure (by legal right).

entries.definition: A particular way or method of doing something, especially one that is distinctive.
examples: The detective recognized the serial burglar by his signature modus operandi.
entries.notes: Often abbreviated as M.O.

entries.definition: Based on first impression; accepted as correct until proved otherwise.
examples: The bank statements provided prima facie evidence of financial fraud.
entries.notes: Latin meaning "at first face".

entries.definition: A favor, benefit, or advantage granted in return for something of equivalent value.
examples: The treaty negotiation involved an intricate quid pro quo between the nations.
entries.notes: Latin for "something for something".

entries.definition: The opinion or beliefs of the majority; the voice of the general public.
examples: Editorial columns often claim to speak directly for the vox populi.
entries.notes: From the proverb "Vox populi, vox Dei" (The voice of the people is the voice of God).

entries.definition: To face a grim or difficult situation with fortitude and courage.
examples: She decided to bite the bullet and give the critical presentation to senior executives.
entries.notes: Historically arose from soldiers biting lead bullets during battlefield surgery.

entries.definition: To relieve tension, stiffness, or awkwardness in a social gathering.
examples: A humorous trivia question helped break the ice among unfamiliar teammates.
entries.notes: Refers to icebreaker ships carving paths for other vessels.

entries.definition: To work, study, or read late into the night with intense focus.
examples: Engineers burned the midnight oil to deploy the patch before market opening.
entries.notes: Refers to burning oil in lamps before the advent of electricity.

entries.term: Hit the nail on the head
entries.definition: To identify or describe the exact root cause of a problem accurately.
examples: Her concise audit of customer churn hit the nail on the head.
entries.notes: Craftsmanship idiom dating back to the 16th century.

entries.term: Let the cat out of the bag
entries.definition: To reveal a secret or confidential piece of information, often accidentally.
examples: David accidentally let the cat out of the bag regarding Maya’s promotion.
entries.notes: Origin debated; commonly linked to marketplace livestock deception.

entries.definition: A task or job that is remarkably simple and easy to do.
examples: After weeks of exhaustive study, the introductory exam was a piece of cake.
entries.notes: Originated in 1930s colloquial American and British English.

entries.definition: To pre-empt someone by doing or saying what they had planned, taking the praise.
examples: Announcing the product launch ahead of her keynote stole her thunder.
entries.notes: Attributed to dramatist John Dennis in 1709 whose theater thunder device was copied.

entries.term: Take with a grain of salt
entries.definition: To view something with a healthy degree of skepticism rather than full acceptance.
examples: Sensational online headlines should always be taken with a grain of salt.
entries.notes: From Latin "cum grano salis", mentioned by Pliny the Elder in 77 AD.

entries.definition: Via gossip, informal hearsay, or rumors passed from person to person.
examples: I heard through the grapevine that a major merger is being finalized.
entries.notes: Traced back to the American Civil War telegraph lines that looked like grapevines.

entries.definition: Feeling slightly ill, indisposed, or lacking usual energy.
examples: He skipped the dinner banquet because he was feeling a bit under the weather.
entries.notes: Nautical origin: sailors retreated below deck in bad weather to rest.

entries.definition: The only true wisdom is in knowing you know nothing.
examples: Socrates
entries.notes: Reflecting the Socratic paradox recorded in Plato’s Apology.

entries.definition: Be the change that you wish to see in the world.
examples: Mahatma Gandhi
entries.notes: Inspiring personal agency and moral leadership.

entries.definition: In the middle of difficulty lies opportunity.
examples: Albert Einstein
entries.notes: Encouraging a growth mindset during adversity.

entries.definition: It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop.
examples: Confucius
entries.notes: Timeless Eastern philosophy on continuous steady progress.

entries.definition: The unexamined life is not worth living.
examples: Socrates
entries.notes: Uttered at Socrates’ trial in Athens.

entries.definition: Stay hungry. Stay foolish. Never settle for what is comfortable.
examples: Steve Jobs (Stanford Commencement, 2005)
entries.notes: Originally published on the back cover of the Whole Earth Catalog in 1974.

entries.definition: Happiness depends upon ourselves.
examples: Aristotle
entries.notes: From Nicomachean Ethics regarding eudaimonia.

entries.definition: Not all those who wander are lost.
examples: J.R.R. Tolkien (The Fellowship of the Ring)
entries.notes: From the poem "All that is gold does not glitter".

entries.definition: He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.
examples: Friedrich Nietzsche
entries.notes: Quoted extensively by Viktor Frankl in Man’s Search for Meaning.

entries.definition: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
examples: Leonardo da Vinci
entries.notes: Guiding principle in timeless architecture, design, and writing.
